Hearing Aid Technology

Most hearing aids that advertise artificial intelligence run a single neural network trained to pull speech out of noise. MaX runs four, each trained on a different job: detecting speech, recognising your own voice, reading the acoustic scene you are standing in, and deciding how to handle the noise. Signia calls the combination Acoustic Intelligence, and the argument is that a system which understands all four dimensions at once behaves more sensibly than one that only knows how to make voices louder.

This page is deliberately more careful than most of what you will read about MaX this month. The platform is days old. Every performance number in circulation traces back to a document Signia wrote, no independent laboratory has measured it, and no price has been published at any level. We have separated what is confirmed from what is claimed from what nobody knows. That is what you actually need in order to decide.

We fit and verify Signia at both our San Mateo and San Carlos offices, and we have fit the Signia range for years. Whether MaX is right for you depends on your audiogram, the rooms you struggle in, and what you need the device to do. Not on how recently it launched. In several situations described below, Signia IX is still the correct choice, and we will tell you so.

At a glance

- Signia MaX (Multi-adaptive Xperience) launched August 24, 2026 with four deep neural networks running together as one system Signia calls Acoustic Intelligence: speech detection, own-voice detection, scene analysis and noise processing.

- Every performance figure comes from Signia's own white papers or from a chip comparison against Signia IX. No independent laboratory has measured MaX, and no price has been published.

- OneConnect puts Bluetooth Classic, LE Audio, telecoil and Auracast in one device. Full Auracast is not enabled until a firmware update due by March 2027.

- It launches in one style only, the rechargeable Pure Charge&Go MaX. For custom, behind-the-ear, instant-fit or CROS fittings, Signia IX remains the platform that can do it, and IX has independent lab scores that MaX does not.

- We fit and verify Signia MaX with real-ear measurement in San Mateo and San Carlos. Verification usually matters more to your result than which platform you choose.

## Four neural networks instead of one

The architectural change is real, and it is worth understanding before you weigh the marketing around it. Signia says MaX runs four deep neural networks simultaneously: one for speech detection, one for own-voice detection, one for scene analysis, and one for noise processing. They are coordinated as a single adaptive system rather than four separate features taking turns. In the wearer-facing language, these surface as RealTime Conversation Enhancement AI, Own Voice Processing AI, Ambient Scene Adaptation AI and Dynamic Noise Control AI. The practical claim behind the architecture is about judgement rather than raw noise reduction. A single-network system knows how to suppress noise; it does not necessarily know whether you are in a conversation, whether the voice it just found is your own, or whether the room changed. Splitting those decisions across purpose-trained networks is meant to stop the device from doing the wrong helpful thing. Muting a restaurant while you are trying to hear the person across the table, say, or ducking your own voice as you speak. Whether that produces a better result in your ears is a separate question, and one no published evidence can yet answer.

## What Signia claims, and who measured it

MaX launched with a short list of striking numbers. We think you should see them with their sources attached rather than as bare facts. Signia reports that 97% of wearers perform better with MaX in noisy group conversations than with key competitors, and that MaX ranks first in signal-to-noise ratio performance in group conversation in noise. Both figures cite white papers authored by Jensen and colleagues in 2026. Those are Signia's own documents, not peer-reviewed publications, and not currently available to read anywhere we can find. The competitors are never named, and the sample size, test protocol and outcome measure are not disclosed. Signia reports that the new MaX chip delivers 54 times more processing power, 50% greater energy efficiency and twice the memory. The footnote attached to that sentence reads, in full, "Compared to Signia IX." That is a baseline statement rather than a citation. There is no study behind it. And Signia reports that RealTime Conversation Enhancement now processes 75% more data points per second than on Signia IX, a figure that carries no footnote at all. None of this makes the claims wrong. Bench measurement and internal validation are how hearing aids get engineered, and Signia's research group has a long record. It does mean nobody outside the company has checked any of it, and that the most impressive-sounding numbers are chip specifications compared against Signia's own previous product rather than evidence about how you will hear.

## What is genuinely confirmed

The hardware picture is clear. MaX launches with one model, the Pure Charge&Go MaX, a rechargeable receiver-in-canal device offered in eight colours. It reached the United States, Germany and the Nordic markets on August 24, 2026, with most remaining markets following later in the year. The charging case is pocket-sized and holds up to four full charges; a full charge takes four hours, and thirty minutes on the charger returns about six hours of use. Connectivity is the standout. Signia calls it OneConnect Technology, and it puts Bluetooth Classic, Bluetooth LE Audio, a telecoil and Auracast into a single device. That combination matters more than it sounds: on Signia IX, choosing a telecoil meant choosing a specific variant, so a patient who needed loop access in a theatre or place of worship gave something up to get it. On MaX there is no such trade-off. Own Voice Processing is also confirmed to work without the in-clinic calibration step IX required, which removes a small but real piece of fitting-day friction.

## The Auracast caveat nobody is printing

Auracast is listed as a MaX feature, and the device is built for it. But it does not fully work yet. Signia's own launch footnote states that full Auracast functionality will be enabled through a firmware update by March 2027. Between now and then, MaX is Auracast-ready rather than Auracast-capable. This is worth knowing because Auracast is being marketed hard across the whole industry right now and very few people are distinguishing between hardware that supports it and hardware on which it currently functions. If broadcast audio in public venues is a reason you are buying, ask about it specifically. For MaX the honest answer today is "soon, and the telecoil works in the meantime," which is not a bad answer, but it is not the same as "yes."

## What MaX cannot do yet

This is the part launch coverage leaves out. MaX exists in one style. There is no custom in-the-ear model, no behind-the-ear model, no Silk-style instant-fit device, no Styletto, no Motion, and no CROS or BiCROS option on the platform. Signia IX offers every one of those, which means that for a patient who needs a powerful behind-the-ear fitting, a custom device for dexterity reasons, an instant-fit tip, or a CROS solution for single-sided deafness, IX is not a compromise. It is the only Signia that can do the job. Signia has also not published a technology-tier structure for MaX, has not published a fitting range or receiver power options, has not stated an IP rating for dust and moisture, and has not announced a price at any level. Notably, no launch material mentions tinnitus therapy at all. Notch Therapy and the static and ocean-wave relief signals are standard across the Signia IX range, so carrying them forward would be the obvious move. But Signia has not said so, and for a practice that treats a great deal of tinnitus we are not going to assume it. We will confirm it in the fitting software and update this page.

## Nobody has measured it. Signia IX has

No independent laboratory has tested Signia MaX. HearAdvisor, the lab whose standardised measurements are the closest thing this industry has to a neutral referee, has published nothing, and neither has anyone else. Based on how previous platform launches have gone, expect a wait of several months. Here is why we raise it rather than glossing over it. Signia IX has been measured, repeatedly and well. HearAdvisor scored the Pure Charge&Go BCT IX at 4.4 out of 5, and the Active Pro IX landed in the top five percent of every product the lab has tested. That is unusually strong independent data, and it belongs to the platform MaX is replacing. So the choice in front of you is not "new and better" against "old and worse." It is a platform with a genuinely new architecture and no external evidence, against a platform with a proven measured record, more styles, and probably a better price once dispensers begin clearing stock. Both are reasonable. Which one is right depends on you, and we would rather have that conversation than sell you the newer box.

## How MaX compares to the other 2026 flagships

MaX did not launch into an empty field. Oticon Reveal arrived two weeks earlier running two AI systems with deliberately opposing objectives, and unlike MaX its Auracast support is live on day one. We set the two side by side on our Signia MaX vs Oticon Reveal page. Phonak's Audéo Infinio Ultra Sphere carries an A grade and a SoundScore of 4.9 out of 5 from HearAdvisor, one of the strongest independent results on the market, but it has no telecoil and no enabled Auracast, which is exactly the gap MaX's OneConnect is aimed at. Phonak replaced that platform with EON on the very same day MaX launched, and EON's Auracast does work today while MaX's waits on firmware. We set the two side by side on our Phonak EON vs Signia MaX page. Starkey Omega AI ranks second of thirty-six devices tested and offers custom in-the-ear styles MaX does not. Widex Allure has no neural network in the sound path at all and still outscores several AI flagships on the bench, which is the clearest evidence available that counting neural networks does not predict how a hearing aid actually performs. We fit all of these, which is why we can afford to be blunt about where each one loses.

## Eight finishes, and why that is not a trivial detail

MaX comes in eight colours: Beige, Black, Chestnut Brown, Dark Champagne, Honey Blonde, Rose Gold, Silver and Titanium Grey. They are identical devices; the finish changes nothing about the sound. We raise it because it is one of the few decisions on this page that is entirely yours, and because it matters more to real patients than the specification sheets suggest. A hearing aid you are self-conscious about is a hearing aid that stays in a drawer, and the single strongest predictor of benefit is hours worn per day. Patients who want the device to disappear against hair or skin usually land on Beige, Honey Blonde or Chestnut Brown; those who would rather it read as a piece of technology than a medical appliance tend to choose Black, Titanium Grey or Silver. We will hold the actual colours against your hair and skin at the fitting rather than asking you to choose from a screen.

## Verified to your prescription, not to the brochure

No platform performs on specification alone. We program MaX to your prescription and confirm it with real-ear measurement . A probe microphone sits in your ear canal and measures what the device actually delivers against your targets across pitches. Then we fine-tune over follow-up visits as your brain adapts. Manufacturer first-fit settings routinely land well below prescriptive targets, which is why an unverified premium device can easily underperform a carefully verified mid-tier one.
